svg.title: The four LLM-judge failure modes and their mitigations
svg.desc: A hand-drawn figure of four cards. Position bias: asked to compare two outputs, the judge prefers whichever came first, strongly enough to flip a large share of verdicts on identical pairs; mitigate by presenting in both orders and averaging, or by scoring absolutely. Length bias: verbose answers score higher even when they are not better; mitigate by normalising rubric items so length is not implicitly rewarded. Self-preference: a judge prefers outputs from its own model family; mitigate by judging with a different family or averaging several judges. Rubric drift: the judge reads the rubric loosely on edge cases until "good" no longer means what it meant at calibration; mitigate by re-calibrating against human labels and versioning the judge prompt. A panel gives the operational rule — publish and version the judge prompt like code — and explains the noise floor: the run-to-run variance that sets the smallest regression worth gating on.
svg.text: Four ways an LLM judge is wrong
Indispensable and treacherous in equal measure. Three of the four were measured in the paper that named the method.
Asked to compare A and B,

average, so a win has to
Publish the judge prompt and version it like code. Many teams treat the judge as infrastructure that does not need review, which is
the same mistake as treating the system prompt as scratch.
Every judged metric has a noise floor: the run-to-run variance when you score the same fixtures twice. Measure it by running the suite twice.
A drop smaller than the noise floor is indistinguishable from a re-roll. Gating on it trains the team to ignore the gate.
